categories.label: Linguistic Sources of Ambiguity and Misinterpretation
categories.memo: Covers specific linguistic phenomena—lexical/syntactic ambiguity, vague terms, jargon, grammar problems—that make contract text unclear and prone to differing interpretations.

codes.label: Lexical and Syntactic Ambiguity
codes.description: Polysemous words and ambiguous sentence structures in contract clauses cause misinterpretation of contractual terminology.

codes.label: Vague and Subjective Terms
codes.description: Use of imprecise words (e.g., 'reasonable', 'inclement weather') allows differing interpretations and opportunistic behavior between parties.

codes.label: Excessive Legal Jargon
codes.description: Contracts drafted by lawyers but used by engineers rely on specialized legal terminology that is difficult for practitioners to comprehend, motivating simplification/NLP-based text simplification research.

codes.label: Grammar and Missing-Noun Problems
codes.description: Attempts to simplify contract language (e.g., NEC abandoning legal jargon) can introduce grammatical errors such as missing nouns, undermining clarity despite good intentions.

codes.label: Sentence Length as Symptom Not Root Cause
codes.description: Shortening sentences, a common readability fix, is a downstream symptom rather than root cause of ambiguity; deeper grammar/terminology issues should be prioritized instead.

codes.label: Negative Language Style
codes.description: Use of negative or adversarial phrasing in clauses reduces trust and collaboration between parties, increasing potential for conflict.

codes.label: Lack of Visual Representation
codes.description: Absence of diagrams, charts and other visual aids in contract documents reduces transparency and is an independent readability risk.

codes.label: Interlinked Scope, Ambiguity and Incoherence
codes.description: Scope complexity, ambiguous wording and incoherence with other clauses/contracts are interconnected root causes that should be addressed together during drafting rather than individually.

categories.label: Completeness and Structural Quality of Contract Requirements
categories.memo: Addresses incompleteness, missing scope definitions, and structural gaps in contract documentation as drivers of disputes, and the challenge of maintaining consistency across requirements.

codes.label: Incomplete Contractual Requirements
codes.description: Contracts with incomplete requirements, especially in subcontracts, lead to design changes, disagreements and disputes among parties.

codes.label: Gaps in Automated Scope Extraction
codes.description: Existing NLP models for classifying/extracting subcontract scope are limited to few disciplines and project types, leaving a gap for comprehensive automated tools applicable to any subcontracted task or project type.

codes.label: Requirement Dependency Tracing
codes.description: No existing tools help trace how a change to one contractual requirement impacts other dependent requirements, risking inconsistency across the contract document.

codes.label: Insufficient Specifications for Modern Methods of Construction
codes.description: Modular/off-site construction lacks separate, adequate specifications compared to conventional construction, contributing to missing-information disputes.

categories.label: Owner vs Contractor Obligation Bias in Drafting
categories.memo: Focuses on how drafting practices and clause content structurally favor one party (typically the owner/client) and how automated tools might detect or quantify this bias.

codes.label: Owner-Inserted Biased or 'Poisonous' Clauses
codes.description: Owners deliberately modify contractual terms and specifications to shift risk onto contractors and other parties, a form of intentional drafting bias.

codes.label: Underexamined Owner Obligations
codes.description: Automated contract review research has focused mainly on contractor obligations, leaving owner obligations (payments, permits, approvals, site information) understudied despite being major dispute sources when unmet.

codes.label: Cross-Standard-Form Obligation Comparison
codes.description: Standard forms (AIA, FIDIC, ConsensusDOCS) differ in how they define and allocate owner obligations; NLP-based comparison across forms could reveal drafting inconsistencies.

codes.label: Numerical Imbalance in Obligation Distribution
codes.description: Quantitative extraction of obligations from clauses reveals that even when raw obligation counts appear balanced, weighted importance can be skewed toward one party (e.g., principal bearing ~15% more importance despite fewer shared obligations).

codes.label: Client Control Over Standard Form Drafting
codes.description: Standard form contracts are typically drafted or heavily influenced by the client/owner, limiting contractor input and skewing risk allocation from the outset.

categories.label: Modification of Standard Forms and Particular Conditions
categories.memo: Examines how amendments, particular conditions and project-specific customization of standard/model contracts affect clarity, risk allocation and readability.

codes.label: Readability Degradation from Customization
codes.description: Modifications made to standard forms (e.g., FIDIC, NEC) by clients to meet project-specific needs tend to reduce overall readability and clarity compared to the unmodified standard form.

codes.label: Relative Clarity of Standard Forms vs Bespoke Contracts
codes.description: Standard forms such as FIDIC and NEC are generally viewed as clearer than traditional bespoke contracts, though each has its own residual readability shortcomings.

codes.label: Functional Stability of Particular Conditions
codes.description: Despite introducing project-specific amendments, particular conditions do not significantly alter the overall functional/risk-distribution profile of the underlying model contract, functioning as coherent extensions rather than redesigns.

codes.label: Interpretation Clauses as Primary Modification Target
codes.description: Interpretation/definition clauses are the most heavily modified subfunction in particular conditions, reflecting drafters' focus on tailoring general definitions to specific project circumstances.

codes.label: Obligation Clarification via Amendments
codes.description: Particular conditions most often add clauses clarifying parties' obligations and task descriptions, an explicit way of assigning responsibility to avert risk before it materializes; such increases may also signal risk transfer that shifts allocation balance.

codes.label: Rigidity of Task-Change Procedures
codes.description: Variation and value-engineering procedures (Task Changes) remain completely unmodified across examined particular conditions, indicating these procedures are treated as fixed regardless of project specifics.

codes.label: Minimal Modification as Best Practice
codes.description: Because stable, widely-used model clauses tend to be efficient, contract managers are advised to make only minor, targeted modifications rather than extensive rewrites when drafting particular conditions.

codes.label: Contract Recycling Without Adaptation
codes.description: Reusing standard contracts from previous projects without properly modifying them for new project conditions is a common industry practice that introduces redundant or inconsistent contractual information.

categories.label: Regulatory and Compliance Language Issues
categories.memo: Concerns the linguistic and procedural challenges of ensuring contract and design compliance with codes and regulations, and the timing of compliance checks.

codes.label: Late-Stage Compliance Checking Limitation
codes.description: Existing NLP compliance-checking models assume complete BIM models and thus only apply at later design phases, when errors are costly to fix; earlier identification of applicable code provisions is needed.

codes.label: Unfamiliarity with Current Codes and Standards
codes.description: Violations of regulatory codes and standards during design, often due to engineers' unfamiliarity with up-to-date codes and inefficient manual compliance checking, are a major source of legal disputes.

categories.label: Analytical and Predictive Tools for Drafting Quality
categories.memo: Covers emerging computational/NLP methods aimed at diagnosing, predicting or improving contract text quality and dispute outcomes, and their current limitations.

codes.label: Litigation Outcome Prediction
codes.description: Predicting litigation outcomes or claim quality before costly court proceedings could help contracting parties negotiate more effectively and avoid disputes.

codes.label: Limited Real-World Validation of NLP Models
codes.description: Existing NLP models for legal/contractual analysis are largely proof-of-concept tested on small or researcher-labeled datasets, limiting scalability and generalizability to real industry contracts and other standard forms like AIA.

codes.label: Root-Cause Hierarchy Approach to Readability
codes.description: Drafting quality improvement should prioritize root causes (grammar, jargon, visual representation, negative language) identified via causal hierarchy analysis rather than addressing surface symptoms individually.

codes.label: Obligation/Risk Extraction Modeling
codes.description: A systematic model for extracting obligations and risk allocation from contract clauses can support drafting parties in achieving a more balanced, risk-aware contract before signing and during administration.

categories.label: Ambiguity Specific to Modern Methods of Construction
categories.memo: Identifies drafting and readability challenges that are distinctive to modular, off-site and industrialized construction methods, not addressed by conventional contract language.

codes.label: Design Limitation Ambiguity from Transportation Constraints
codes.description: In modular construction, design choices are constrained by transportation/shipment methods, creating ambiguity around design limitations, standardization, and module interfacing not present in conventional construction contract language.

codes.label: Missing Guidance on Fault-Tolerant Module Design
codes.description: Contracts lack clear provisions requiring fault-tolerant design systems to reduce on-site rework caused by assembly interface problems between prefabricated modules.

codes.label: External Factors Unaddressed by Contract Drafting
codes.description: Volumetric transportation difficulties, contradictory transport regulations across jurisdictions, and absent building codes for modular construction are significant sources of ambiguity not addressed in current contract frameworks.

codes.label: Industry Maturity Considerations Absent from Drafting
codes.description: The level of local industry maturity and adoption of modern/efficient construction practices strongly affects project progress and should be considered in contract drafting, yet is rarely addressed explicitly.

codes.label: Procurement Strategy as Ambiguity Driver
codes.description: Sources of contractual ambiguity and confusion are strongly correlated with the chosen procurement strategy and delivery method, an interaction not well captured in current standard contract drafting.
